01

Setting specification

Task

Find an approximately stationary point of the reduced objective $\Phi$, obtained by maximizing the payoff over the second block. Return the primal point $\widehat x$.

$$ \min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x}}\Phi(x),\qquad\Phi(x)=\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}}f(x,y). $$

Admissible model

$f:\mathbb{R}^{d_x}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_y}\to\mathbb{R}$, with both blocks unconstrained and Euclidean norms throughout. The joint gradient satisfies $\|\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(w)\|_2\le \beta\|z-w\|_2$.

For every $x$, $f(x,\cdot)$ is uniformly $\mu_y$-strongly concave. Thus $y^\star(x)=\arg\max_y f(x,y)$ is unique and $\Phi(x)=f(x,y^\star(x))$ is differentiable. Neither $f(\cdot,y)$ nor $\Phi$ is assumed convex.

Assume $\inf_x\Phi(x)>-\infty$, with an initial point satisfying $\Phi(x_0)-\inf_x\Phi(x)\le\Delta$.

The initial point $(x_0,y_0)=(0,0)$ is public. There is no uniform upper bound on $\|\nabla_y f(0,0)\|_2$, $\|y_0-y^\star(x_0)\|_2$, or the dual gap.

The dimension $d_x,d_y$ is a finite positive integer visible to the algorithm. Complexity takes a uniform worst case over these dimensions. Candidate budgets may not depend on the hidden instance’s dual-initialization scale.

Oracle interface

Public inputs include block dimensions $d_x,d_y$ and $\Delta$, $\beta$, $\varepsilon$, and $\mu_y$, together with the stated initial-point and feasible-domain information. Analytic representations of hidden functions, operators, or matrices are not revealed.

$$ (x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_y}\longmapsto (\nabla_x f(x,y),\nabla_y f(x,y)) $$

Responses are exact and noiseless; neither function values nor Hessians are returned.

The interface does not directly supply $y^\star(x)$, $\Phi(x)$, or $\nabla\Phi(x)$. Every primitive gradient used for inner optimization is charged.

Output

Return a single $\widehat x\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$. No dual point is required.

The output may be any measurable postprocessing of the history, including an unqueried point, average, or convex combination. It must satisfy the stated domain and feasibility requirements; no additional function value or computable certificate is required.

Loss or accuracy criterion

Accuracy is the Euclidean norm of the gradient of the reduced objective at the returned primal point. For each admissible instance, the norm must be at most $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $2/3$.

$$ \|\nabla\Phi(\widehat{x})\|_2 $$

The identity $\nabla\Phi(x)=\nabla_xf(x,y^\star(x))$ specifies the evaluation target and does not supply an additional Oracle interface.

Resource accounting

One full joint gradient costs one $N_{\mathrm{grad}}$ call. Both blocks are returned together, not charged as two calls.

Use a fixed worst-case budget: calls never exceed the prespecified $N$ on any instance or random execution path. Earlier stopping within the budget is permitted.

Here $+\infty$ means that for every finite candidate budget $N$, some finite dimension and admissible instance prevent any $N$-call algorithm from achieving success probability $2/3$. It does not assert that every fixed finite-dimensional instance is unsolvable or requires infinitely many calls.

Count all information calls for one instance and one requested accuracy, including initialization. Exact-real arithmetic, storage, and solving known models from public inputs and returned data are uncharged. This query-complexity quantity does not certify arithmetic or bit complexity.

Algorithm views and success guarantees

Arbitrary measurable sequential adaptive randomized algorithms are allowed. The private seed is independent of the hidden instance. Queries, stopping, and output may use the full history, without additional span, zero-respecting, communication, or memory restrictions.

A single algorithm is chosen from the public input and must satisfy the guarantee for every fixed admissible instance.

$$ \Pr\!\left(\|\nabla\Phi(\widehat{x})\|_2\le\varepsilon\right)\ge\frac23. $$

Probability is over private algorithmic randomness only. The unknown instance is fixed before interaction.

Budget convention
fixed worst-case query cap

Notation and parameters

$\Delta$

A public bound on the initial reduced-objective value above its infimum. Attainment of the infimum is not required.

Domain
Positive real number

$\Phi(0)-\inf_x\Phi(x)\le\Delta$

$\beta$

Euclidean Lipschitz upper bound for the population payoff's complete joint gradient.

Domain
Positive real number

$\|\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(w)\|_2\le\beta\|z-w\|_2$

$d$

The joint Euclidean dimension is $d=d_x+d_y$. Within its stated window, the lower bound may choose finite block dimensions.

Domain
Integer at least $2$
$\varepsilon$

Euclidean norm tolerance for the true reduced gradient; the mean-square contract targets its square $\varepsilon^2$.

Domain
Positive real number
$\kappa$

Ratio of the population smoothness upper bound, or mean-square average smoothness for finite sums, to the dual strong-concavity lower bound

Domain
$\kappa\ge1$

$\kappa=\beta/\mu_y$

$\mu_y$

A uniform strong-convexity lower bound for −f(x,·) at every fixed x; equivalently, the dual strong-concavity modulus of f.

Domain
$0<\mu_y\le\beta$

$f(x,v)\le f(x,y)+\langle\nabla_yf(x,y),v-y\rangle-\frac{\mu_y}{2}\|v-y\|_2^2$

$\|\cdot\|_2,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$

Euclidean norm and inner product; the product-space norm is the square root of the sum of the squared block norms.

Domain
The specified finite-dimensional real vector space.

$\|v\|_2=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$

$d_x,d_y$

Positive integer primal and dual block dimensions; joint dimension $d=d_x+d_y$

Domain
Positive integer
$f$

Unknown real-valued payoff, with primal and dual input blocks.

Domain
$f:(x,y)\mapsto f(x,y)\in\mathbb R$
$x,y,z$

Primal variable, dual variable, and joint point

Domain
$x\in\mathbb R^{d_x},\ y\in\mathbb R^{d_y},\ z=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{d_x+d_y}$

$z=(x,y)$

$\nabla f,\nabla_x f,\nabla_y f$

Complete joint gradient and its two blocks

Domain
$\nabla_x f\in\mathbb R^{d_x},\ \nabla_y f\in\mathbb R^{d_y}$

$\nabla f=(\nabla_x f,\nabla_y f)$

$\Phi$

Reduced objective after global dual maximization; neither its value nor gradient is an additional free interface

Domain
Real-valued function on the primal-variable space

$\Phi(x)=\max_{y\in \mathbb R^{d_y}}f(x,y)$

$y^\star(x)$

The unique global dual maximizer at fixed primal x.

Domain
$y^\star(x)\in\mathbb R^{d_y}$

$y^\star(x)=\arg\max_{y\in\mathbb R^{d_y}}f(x,y)$

$x_0,y_0$

The public initial primal and dual variables.

Domain
The respective feasible domains. Both equal zero when the origins are explicitly fixed.
$\widehat x$

The point or variable blocks ultimately returned by the algorithm, corresponding to the hatted variables in the error formula.

Domain
A feasible primal point in $\mathbb R^{d_x}$.

Complexity bracket

Each bracket applies to the stated view, success guarantee, resource and parameter region. Status summarizes the documented comparisons.

Compared quantities and resource definitions

Q1 · target accuracy cost

\[N^\star=\inf_{\mathcal A\in\mathfrak A_{\rm succ}}\ \sup_{d_x,d_y\ge1}\ \sup_{I\in\mathcal F_{d_x,d_y}}\ \sup_\omega N_{\mathcal A}(I,\omega)\]
Scope
The algorithm may read the finite block dimensions. A single algorithm family must succeed with probability at least $2/3$ on every admissible instance, with a budget uniform over all finite dimensions. If no successful algorithm family or uniform finite budget exists, the complexity is $+\infty$.
Optimization direction
minimize

The algorithm class is exactly the declared legal algorithms attaining the adjacent specification guarantee; C is the declared charged resource projection. Expected-call objectives retain E N; fixed budgets take worst-case execution cost. The instance/oracle class and dimension regime remain those in the specification.

B1

Two-ended dual chain with exact gradients: independent fair signs and a random orthogonal frame

Sharp Fresh-Gradient Complexity of Nonconvex--Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization ↗
Conditions
Assume $\beta\ge4\mu_y>0$, $\varepsilon>0$, and $\Delta\ge80\varepsilon^2/\beta$; $\|\nabla_yf(0,0)\|_2$ is unrestricted.; The noiseless hard instances in Theorem 3.6 already belong to this exact joint-gradient model. Neither stochastic oracle noise nor a linear-span restriction is needed.; The hard distribution in Appendix B is fixed before interaction and independent of the algorithmic seed. At every finite budget $N$, average success probability is at most $7/12$. Hence some fixed admissible instance has success probability below $2/3$.
Dimension conditions
For each $N\ge1$, choose $d_x=1$ and chain length $m=4N+4$. Equation (20) of Theorem B.2 supplies a sufficiently large finite $d_y$. Both $d_y$ and initial dual residual may grow with $N$. Infinite complexity at fixed $d_y$ is not proved.
Algorithm scope
Any measurable adaptive randomized queries and measurable final primal output are allowed. Query vectors may be dense, nonlinear, and unbounded in norm. The fixed budget applies to every execution path.
Correspondence, constants and qualifications
Oracle correspondence
Each call returns both gradient blocks exactly. The source hard construction supplies no function values, Hessians, inner solutions, or reduced gradients, matching this interface exactly.
Guarantee conversion
The success event is $\|\nabla\Phi(\widehat x)\|_2\le\varepsilon$, with probability over the algorithmic seed only. A distribution-average success upper bound establishes failure on at least one fixed instance.
Output rule
The successful primal-output intervals for the two hidden signs are disjoint. The output argument in Theorem B.2 allows unqueried points of arbitrary norm.
Resource conversion
A uniform finite integer N bounds all joint-gradient calls on every instance and every execution path. It is not a worst-instance expected stopping time.
Constants
Use the source theorem’s universal constants except where derivative order or structural budgets are explicitly fixed. Unspecified sufficient thresholds remain symbolic.
Logarithmic factors
None.
Scope qualification
Definition 3.2 and Theorem B.2 explicitly allow arbitrary randomized adaptive unbounded queries and unqueried outputs.
Upper bound

Infinite complexity

Comparison argument
Without dual-initialization control, every finite budget admits an admissible finite-dimensional instance on which the algorithm fails. This is an impossibility result, not a missing search result.
